title: First-Time Donor? Here Is Exactly Where to Start
excerpt: Making your first charitable gift can feel overwhelming. Here's a plain-language guide to finding a cause, verifying a charity, and making a gift that actually matters.
content:
Starting Is the Hard Part

Every generous person faces the same moment: you want to give, but you don't know where to begin. There are roughly 86,000 registered charities in Canada. The causes are endless. The asks are constant. And the fear of giving to the wrong organization stops a lot of people from giving at all.

Here's what we know: the perfect is the enemy of the good. A thoughtful first gift — even a small one — is infinitely better than endlessly researching and never clicking the donate button. This guide will help you take that first step with confidence.

Step 1: Start With What Already Moves You

The most sustainable giving comes from a genuine connection to a cause. Think about the people in your life, the experiences that have shaped you, the news stories that have stayed with you. Are you drawn to health research because a family member has faced illness? To youth programs because of a mentor who changed your life? To environmental causes because of the world you want to leave behind?

You don't need to solve the world's biggest problem on your first gift. You just need to start somewhere real.

Step 2: Verify Before You Give

Canada's CRA (Canada Revenue Agency) maintains a public registry of all registered charities. Before you donate to any organization, you can look it up at canada.ca/charities-giving. A registered charity has a unique Business Number (BN) — typically in the format 123456789 RR 0001 — and must file annual T3010 returns that show how they spend their money.

Key things to check: Is the charity registered and in good standing? What percentage of spending goes to programs versus administration? Does the charity publish audited financial statements?

Step 3: Decide How Much and How Often

There's no right answer for how much to give. Some donors use a percentage of income as their guide — even 1% is meaningful. Others give around significant life events, or match a monthly subscription cost as a benchmark.

Consider starting with a monthly gift rather than a one-time donation. Charities strongly prefer recurring donors because it allows them to plan programs and reduce fundraising costs. A $25/month donor contributes $300 per year — more than most one-time gifts — and the habit tends to stick.

Step 4: Keep Your Receipt

Canadian charities are required to issue official donation receipts for gifts of $10 or more. Keep every receipt — you'll need them at tax time. Federal tax credits for charitable donations are among the most generous in the OECD, and provincial credits stack on top. Your $300 in annual gifts could reduce your tax bill by $85 or more.

You're Ready

Choose one cause. Find one registered charity. Make one gift. That's all it takes to begin a giving practice. The rest — how much, how often, which strategies to use — can be refined over time. The important thing is to start.

title: How to Evaluate a Charity Before You Give
excerpt: Not all charities are equal. Here's a practical framework for researching any organization before you donate — using free Canadian tools.
content:
Why Research Matters

Most Canadian charities are doing genuine, important work. But donors deserve to understand how their dollars are being used. A bit of research before your first gift to any organization builds trust — and it helps you give more strategically over time.

The good news: Canada has one of the most transparent charity reporting systems in the world. With a few simple tools, you can learn a great deal about any registered charity for free.

Start With the CRA Charity Listing

Every registered Canadian charity must file an annual T3010 Registered Charity Information Return with the CRA. These filings are publicly available at canada.ca/charities-giving and show:

  • Total revenues and how they were raised
  • Total expenditures broken down by program, management, and fundraising
  • The charity's stated programs and activities
  • Names of directors and key staff
  • Whether the charity is in good standing

Look up any charity by name or BN number and review at least two years of filings. You're looking for consistency, growth, and clarity.

Look at the Program-to-Admin Ratio — But Carefully

One popular metric is the ratio of program spending to administrative and fundraising costs. A charity that spends 90 cents of every dollar on programs is generally more efficient than one that spends 50 cents. But this ratio can be misleading. A startup charity may have higher overhead as it builds capacity. A charity that invests in fundraising may generate far more revenue — and do far more good — than one that cuts every administrative cost.

Use the ratio as one data point, not the whole picture.

Check for Audited Financial Statements

Mid-sized and large charities should publish annual audited financial statements. An independent audit provides assurance that the numbers are accurate and that accounting standards are being followed. If a charity can't or won't share audited financials, that's a reason to ask more questions.

Read Their Annual Report

Most established charities publish an annual report that goes beyond the numbers. Look for concrete outcomes: how many people served, what changed because of their programs, what challenges they're facing. Organizations that can articulate their impact clearly are usually doing more rigorous work.

Trust Your Instincts

If something feels off — vague language about programs, high-pressure fundraising tactics, no clear mission statement, or an inability to explain what they do — pay attention to that feeling. The best charities are transparent, responsive to donor questions, and eager to share their results. When in doubt, give to an organization you've been able to vet thoroughly.

title: Understanding Your Charitable Tax Receipt
excerpt: Your donation receipt is worth more than you might think. Here's exactly how Canadian charitable tax credits work — and what to do with your receipts at tax time.
content:
What Is an Official Donation Receipt?

When you donate to a registered Canadian charity, you're entitled to receive an official donation receipt for the full amount of your gift (minus any benefit you receive in return). This receipt isn't just a thank-you note — it's a tax document that can meaningfully reduce your federal and provincial tax bill.

The CRA requires that official donation receipts include specific information: the charity's name, registered BN number, the date and amount of the gift, the donor's name and address, and a statement that it is an official receipt for income tax purposes. If any of these are missing, the receipt may not be valid for tax purposes.

How the Federal Tax Credit Works

Canada's charitable donation tax credit is calculated on your federal return as follows:

  • 15% on the first $200 of total donations in a tax year
  • 29% on amounts above $200 (33% if your income is in the top bracket)

This means if you donate $1,000 in a year, your federal credit is ($200 × 15%) + ($800 × 29%) = $30 + $232 = $262. Add in provincial credits (which vary by province but typically add another 5–20%) and your total tax savings could be well over $300.

Stacking Receipts for Maximum Impact

One powerful strategy: consolidate your family's donations on one tax return. In Canada, spouses can pool all donation receipts and claim them on either return. It's almost always more advantageous to claim all receipts on the higher-income spouse's return, as the 29% (or 33%) federal rate kicks in above $200 total — not $200 per person.

You can also carry forward unclaimed donation receipts for up to five years. If your income is lower this year, you may get a higher credit by claiming those receipts in a future year when you're in a higher tax bracket.

Gifts in Kind

For non-cash donations — like donated securities, art, or property — the receipt should show the fair market value at the time of the gift. If you donate publicly traded shares that have appreciated in value, the receipt is for the full fair market value, and you pay no capital gains tax on the gain. This is one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available to Canadians.

Keep Every Receipt

Store your donation receipts in a dedicated folder — digital or physical. You'll need them if the CRA ever asks to verify your charitable donation claims. The CRA may audit these claims, and without a valid receipt, the tax credit can be disallowed.

title: How Much Should You Give? Finding a Number That Feels Right
excerpt: There is no objectively correct amount to give. But there are frameworks — rooted in research and centuries of tradition — that can help you find a number that works for your life.
content:
The Question Nobody Wants to Answer Directly

Ask a financial advisor how much you should donate and most will change the subject. Ask a charity and they'll give you a number that makes you feel either guilty or exhilarated. Ask a philosopher and you'll get a seminar.

We'll try to be more useful than that.

The Tithe: 10% as a Starting Point

The practice of giving 10% of one's income to community and charitable causes has roots in virtually every major religious tradition. In modern secular usage, giving 10% of your gross income is considered a meaningful benchmark — ambitious for most people, but achievable for those who prioritize it.

Organizations like Giving What We Can encourage donors to pledge at least 10% of their income. Research by the Charitable Giving Research Fund suggests that Canadians who give at this level report significantly higher life satisfaction than those who give less — or not at all.

1% as a Meaningful Floor

If 10% feels out of reach, 1% of gross income is a defensible and meaningful floor. On a $60,000 salary, that's $600 per year — about $50 per month. Combined with tax credits, the after-tax cost is closer to $35 per month. At that level, you're making a real difference without financial strain.

The Subscription Heuristic

Here's a practical approach: match your charitable giving to a recurring subscription you value. If you spend $15/month on a streaming service, what would it look like to match that with a $15/month donation? Most Canadians spend significantly more on subscriptions and conveniences than they give charitably — and the difference in wellbeing between those two expenditures is striking.

Make It Automatic

The single most effective strategy for maintaining a giving practice is automation. Set up a monthly donation that comes out of your account the same day as other fixed expenses. You stop thinking about it as a choice each month and start treating it as a non-negotiable — like rent or car insurance.

When you automate your giving, you also insulate yourself from giving fatigue. You won't feel guilty every time a charity asks for money because you already have a plan.

Revisit Annually

Build in an annual giving review. Each year, ask yourself: does my giving still reflect my values? Have my finances changed? Are the organizations I support doing the work I care about? This doesn't need to be a major exercise — even a 30-minute review each January can keep your philanthropy intentional and growing.

title: What Is a Registered Charity? A Plain-Language Explainer
excerpt: Not every good-cause organization qualifies as a registered charity. Here's what the CRA designation actually means — and why it matters for your donation.
content:
Two Words That Matter at Tax Time

When you donate to an organization, you might assume you'll automatically get a tax receipt. But that's only the case if the organization is a registered charity with the CRA. The designation matters — both for your tax return and as a signal about the organization's accountability.

What Makes an Organization a Registered Charity?

To become registered, a Canadian charity must apply to the CRA and demonstrate that it meets three requirements:

  1. It has exclusively charitable purposes — broadly defined as relief of poverty, advancement of education, advancement of religion, or other purposes that benefit the community in a legally recognized way.
  2. It carries out charitable activities that further those purposes.
  3. It is legally constituted and not-for-profit, with no private benefit to shareholders or founders.

Once registered, the charity receives a Business Number (BN) in the format XXXXXXXXX RR 000X, must file annual T3010 returns, and is subject to CRA oversight.

What You Can Do With a Registered Charity

Only registered charities can issue official tax receipts for donations. This is the key practical difference from other non-profit organizations. When you donate to a registered charity, you get a receipt you can use to claim federal and provincial tax credits. When you donate to an unregistered non-profit — even a genuinely worthy one — you typically don't.

Types of Registered Charities

The CRA recognizes three categories: charitable organizations (usually hands-on service providers), public foundations (primarily grant-making with a broad base of support), and private foundations (grant-making controlled by a family or small group). Donors can give to all three and receive receipts in all cases.

How to Verify a Charity's Registration

The CRA's publicly searchable registry at canada.ca/charities-giving lets anyone verify a charity's registration status, BN number, and filing history. Always verify before you donate. If an organization claims to be a registered charity but can't provide a BN, treat that as a red flag.

When a Good Organization Isn't Registered

Some organizations — particularly newer nonprofits, mutual aid networks, and advocacy groups — do important work without CRA registration. Giving to them may not generate a tax receipt, but it's not inherently problematic. The key is to be clear-eyed about what you're getting and make an informed decision.

title: Why Donating Stocks Instead of Cash Saves You Money
excerpt: If you hold appreciated securities, donating them directly to a registered charity eliminates capital gains tax entirely — making this one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available to Canadians.
content:
The Problem With Selling First

Suppose you bought shares five years ago for $5,000 and they're now worth $15,000. You want to donate the proceeds. If you sell the shares, you'll realize a $10,000 capital gain. In Canada, 50% of that gain ($5,000) is added to your taxable income. At a 40% marginal rate, that's $2,000 in capital gains tax — before you've even made the donation.

Then you donate the $15,000 in cash and receive a donation tax credit. The credit helps, but you still paid $2,000 in tax you didn't need to pay.

The Better Approach: Donate the Shares Directly

Under Canadian tax law, when you donate publicly traded securities directly to a registered charity — without selling them first — the capital gains inclusion rate on those securities drops to zero. You pay no capital gains tax on the gain, and you receive a donation receipt for the full fair market value of the shares on the date of the gift.

In the example above, donating $15,000 of shares directly gives you a $15,000 receipt and no capital gains tax. The tax saving on the gain alone is $2,000 — money that effectively goes to the charity (or stays in your pocket for future giving) rather than to the government.

What Securities Qualify?

The zero-inclusion rule applies to shares listed on a designated stock exchange, mutual fund units, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), interests in segregated funds, and certain other eligible investments. It does not apply to private company shares, real estate, or cryptocurrency (though proposed legislation has been introduced regarding crypto on multiple occasions).

How the Process Works

Contact the charity and let them know you want to donate securities. They'll provide their brokerage account information (DTC instructions or Canadian equivalent). You then instruct your broker to transfer the shares directly — not sold, transferred in-kind. The charity sells the shares upon receipt, and you receive a receipt for the FMV on the transfer date. The process typically takes 3–7 business days once initiated.

Year-End Planning

If you plan to donate securities, initiate the transfer by mid-December to ensure it settles before year-end. Many brokers get backed up in December, and a transfer that doesn't settle until January means your receipt falls in the next tax year. Build in extra time and confirm the expected settlement date with your broker.

For donors with non-registered investment accounts holding appreciated securities, this is the single most tax-efficient giving strategy available under Canadian law. Speak with a financial advisor or tax professional to incorporate it into your overall plan.

title: The Donor-Advised Fund: Canada's Best-Kept Charitable Secret
excerpt: A donor-advised fund lets you take your charitable tax deduction now and decide which charities to support later. Here's how they work and who should consider one.
content:
What Is a Donor-Advised Fund?

A donor-advised fund (DAF) is a charitable account that you fund with an irrevocable gift — cash, securities, or other eligible assets — and from which you recommend grants to registered charities over time. The key feature: you get the tax receipt at the time of contribution, not when you make grants to individual charities.

In Canada, DAFs are offered by community foundations (such as the Vancouver Foundation, the Calgary Foundation, or the Toronto Foundation), some national foundations, and financial institutions like Fidelity Charitable Canada.

How It Works in Practice

You open a DAF account with a sponsoring organization and make an initial contribution — often a minimum of $10,000–$25,000, though some programs have lower thresholds. The contribution is irrevocable: it legally belongs to the sponsoring organization from that point on, though you retain advisory rights over how it's invested and distributed.

The sponsoring organization invests your contribution, typically in a range of balanced or growth-oriented pools. The account can grow tax-free. When you want to support a charity, you submit a grant recommendation to the sponsoring organization, which then disburses the funds on your behalf. Most sponsoring organizations process grants within a few business days.

Why They're Powerful for Donors

DAFs are especially useful in three situations. First, when you have a high-income year — from selling a business, exercising options, or a large bonus — and want to capture the tax credit in that year even if you haven't identified all the charities you want to support. Second, when you're donating appreciated securities and want a single transaction rather than multiple stock transfers to different charities. Third, when you want to build a structured giving practice that gradually deploys a pool of funds over many years.

Fees and Minimums

DAF sponsors typically charge an annual administrative fee of 0.5–1.0% of assets, plus investment management fees on underlying funds. These fees are paid from within the fund, not out of pocket. Over time, if the fund grows faster than the fee rate, this can actually amplify the total dollars available for grants.

A Starting Point for Structured Philanthropy

For donors who want to take their giving seriously but aren't ready to establish a private foundation, a DAF offers many of the same benefits at a fraction of the cost and administrative burden. It's a legitimate way to separate the financial decision (funding the account) from the philanthropic decision (choosing charities) — which often makes both decisions better.

title: Matching Gifts: Free Money Your Employer May Be Leaving on the Table
excerpt: Many Canadian employers will match employee charitable donations — some dollar for dollar, others 2:1 or more. Here's how to find out if your company has a program and how to use it.
content:
What Is a Matching Gift Program?

An employer matching gift program is a benefit that allows employees to multiply the impact of their personal charitable donations. When you donate to an eligible charity, your employer makes an additional donation — typically matching yours dollar for dollar, though some programs match at higher ratios.

According to Double the Donation, approximately 65% of Fortune 500 companies in North America offer matching gift programs. In Canada, major employers in banking, insurance, consulting, technology, and resource sectors frequently offer these programs. Yet research consistently shows that the majority of eligible employees never submit a matching gift request.

How to Find Out If Your Employer Participates

Start with HR. Many employers publicize matching programs through their intranet or benefits portal but don't actively advertise them in day-to-day communications. Ask your HR department directly: Does the company offer charitable donation matching? What are the eligible charities and maximum annual match amounts?

If your company hasn't established a program, you may be able to suggest one. Employee-led proposals for matching gift programs are relatively common and often successful, especially in companies with active CSR (corporate social responsibility) initiatives.

How the Process Typically Works

The specifics vary by employer, but the typical process is: you donate to an eligible charity, obtain your official donation receipt, then submit a matching gift request through your HR portal or a third-party platform your employer uses (common platforms include Benevity, YourCause, and Cybergrants). Your employer reviews the submission and sends a matching gift to the charity directly.

Some employers match at year-end; others process requests throughout the year. Note that some programs cap the annual match per employee — often between $500 and $5,000 per year.

Volunteer Grant Programs

Beyond cash matching, many employers also offer volunteer grants — donations made to charities where employees volunteer. If you volunteer 10+ hours at a local food bank, your employer might donate $100–$500 to that organization on your behalf. Check whether your employer offers this benefit alongside donation matching.

The Bottom Line

If your employer has a matching gift program and you're not using it, you're leaving money on the table — money that could double your charitable impact at no additional cost to you. This is one of the simplest and highest-return actions any donor can take. Check your HR portal today.

title: Giving Circles: Pool Your Dollars, Multiply Your Impact
excerpt: A giving circle is a group of donors who pool their money and collectively decide which charities to support. They're growing in Canada — and for good reason.
content:
What Is a Giving Circle?

A giving circle is a form of participatory philanthropy in which a group of people pool their donations and collectively decide which organizations to fund. Members typically contribute a set amount per year — anywhere from $100 to several thousand dollars — and the group distributes the pooled funds through a democratic or consensus-based process.

Giving circles aren't new. Informal community giving pools have existed for centuries across many cultures. What's changed is that they've become more structured, more diverse, and more explicitly focused on learning and community-building alongside grant-making.

Why They Work

The appeal of giving circles is multiple. Pooling modest individual contributions can fund grants large enough to make a real difference to smaller organizations that rarely receive attention from institutional funders. Members learn from each other — a giving circle is an education in philanthropy, not just a funding mechanism. And the social dimension — gathering with people who share your values and deliberating about where to give — tends to deepen and sustain giving habits in ways that solo donating often doesn't.

How Canadian Giving Circles Are Structured

Some giving circles operate informally among friends or colleagues. Others are structured as funds within a community foundation, which handles the administration and provides charitable receipts. A growing number are organized around specific communities — women's giving circles, immigrant community circles, and sector-specific circles focused on the environment or arts.

Key design decisions include: Who is eligible to join? How are grant decisions made? How often does the group meet? What's the minimum contribution? Whether decisions require consensus, majority vote, or rotating leadership all affect the culture of the circle.

Starting or Joining One

If you want to join an existing giving circle, start with your local community foundation — most maintain a registry of active circles in their region. Organizations like Philanthropic Foundations Canada and the Giving Circles Network Canada can also point you toward existing groups.

If you want to start one, you need only three things: a committed group of co-founders, a decision-making framework, and a mechanism for pooling donations (often a fund at a community foundation). Many circles start with as few as five people and expand through word of mouth.

Who Giving Circles Are For

Giving circles work particularly well for donors who want to give more strategically but don't have the time or assets to research individual charities thoroughly. They're also excellent for first-time donors looking for a structured introduction to philanthropy, and for donors who want the social and educational dimensions of giving — not just the transaction.

title: Overhead Ratios: Why the Efficiency Myth Hurts Good Charities
excerpt: The obsession with low overhead ratios has caused enormous harm to Canada's charitable sector. Here's what the research actually says — and better questions to ask instead.
content:
The Problem With the Overhead Narrative

For decades, the dominant narrative in charitable giving has been: good charities spend as little as possible on administration and fundraising, directing nearly every dollar to programs. Rating agencies built their entire models on this premise. Donors internalized the message so deeply that many still judge a charity's worthiness primarily by its overhead ratio.

The problem? The evidence doesn't support this framework — and it actively encourages behaviours that hurt the charities donors care most about.

What the Research Shows

A landmark study by the Stanford Social Innovation Review found no evidence that lower overhead ratios are associated with better outcomes for the people charities serve. In fact, charities that underspend on infrastructure often deliver worse programs, burn out staff, and fail to scale. An organization that spends 25% on administration but delivers measurably strong outcomes is doing better work than one that spends 5% but can't demonstrate any impact.

Charity watchdog organizations like Charity Navigator — which built its reputation on overhead analysis — have largely moved away from overhead ratios as a primary metric, instead focusing on results-oriented assessment. Candid (formerly GuideStar) made a similar shift. Canadian donors deserve to make the same upgrade.

The Real Costs of the Overhead Myth

When donors penalize charities for overhead, charities respond rationally: they underinvest in the things that would make them more effective. They defer technology upgrades, cut staff training, underpay skilled professionals (contributing to sector-wide talent loss), and even misclassify program costs as administrative costs to keep their ratios artificially low. None of this serves the people they're trying to help.

Better Questions to Ask

Instead of asking

, try asking: What outcomes does this charity achieve, and how do they measure them? Has it demonstrated improvement over time? Does it attract and retain talented staff? Is it financially sustainable? Does it publish detailed program reports?

A charity with 20% overhead that can answer these questions clearly is almost always a better investment than a charity with 5% overhead that can't.

Still Worth Watching — In Extremes

This isn't to say overhead ratios are meaningless. A charity that spends 60% on fundraising and 40% on programs should raise questions. But in the normal range — roughly 10–30% — overhead tells you very little about quality. Use it as a flag at the extremes, not as a primary measure of worth.

title: Giving to Indigenous-Led Organizations: A Guide to Giving With Respect
excerpt: Supporting Indigenous communities in Canada is an act of reconciliation — but it requires understanding who to give to, how to give respectfully, and what to avoid.
content:
Why This Guide Exists

The history of charitable giving toward Indigenous peoples in Canada is complicated by colonialism, paternalism, and well-meaning but harmful interventions. Many legacy organizations that served Indigenous communities were not led by Indigenous people and reflected the priorities of the dominant culture rather than the communities themselves. Reconciliation requires a different approach.

Start With Indigenous-Led

The most important principle: prioritize organizations that are led by and accountable to Indigenous communities. This means Indigenous people are in senior leadership and on the board, program decisions are made with genuine community input, and the organization's governance reflects Indigenous values and priorities.

Organizations like Indspire (scholarships for First Nations, Inuit, and Métis students), the First Nations Child & Family Caring Society, and Reconciliation Canada are prominent examples. Local urban Indigenous organizations — friendship centres, women's shelters, youth programs — are often underfunded and doing essential work.

Understand the Distinctions

Canada's Indigenous population is not monolithic. There are more than 630 First Nations communities, dozens of Inuit communities and Métis organizations, and hundreds of languages, cultures, and governance systems. A donation to a national organization may not reach the specific community you care about. Research the geography and governance of any organization you're considering.

Unrestricted Giving Is Often Most Valuable

Many Indigenous-led organizations operate with chronic underfunding and over-restricted grants from government and foundations. Unrestricted donations — those that can be used where the organization sees the greatest need — are often more valuable than project-specific gifts. When you give without conditions, you express trust and respect for the organization's leadership.

Avoid Extractive Giving Patterns

Be cautious of organizations — often non-Indigenous-led — that use Indigenous imagery or stories primarily to generate donations, without substantive Indigenous leadership or accountability. Ask: Who sits on the board? Who makes program decisions? What percentage of leadership is Indigenous? Is the community they serve involved in governance?

Amplify, Don't Replace

Your donation is most powerful when it amplifies what Indigenous communities are already doing — not when it imposes priorities from outside. The best Indigenous-led organizations will tell you what they need. Listen to them.

title: Your RRSP, RRIF, and Your Favourite Charity
excerpt: Naming a registered charity as the beneficiary of your RRSP or RRIF at the time of your passing can eliminate tens of thousands of dollars in taxes. Here's how it works.
content:
The Tax Problem With RRSPs and RRIFs

Most Canadians know that RRSP and RRIF assets are tax-deferred — you contribute pre-tax dollars, invest tax-free, and pay income tax when you withdraw. What many don't realize is the full magnitude of the tax event that occurs when you pass away.

When the last surviving account holder of an RRSP or RRIF passes away, the entire remaining balance is deemed to have been received as income in the year of passing. A $500,000 RRIF could generate $250,000 or more in income tax on a final return — potentially at the highest marginal rates.

The Charitable Beneficiary Solution

By naming a registered charity as the direct beneficiary of your RRSP or RRIF — or leaving the assets to your estate with direction to donate them — you can generate a charitable donation tax credit on your final return that offsets the income inclusion. Under Canadian tax law, the estate of a deceased taxpayer can claim charitable donation credits up to 100% of net income in the year of passing and the preceding year.

This means a $300,000 RRSP donated to charity on the passing of the last holder generates a $300,000 donation credit — which can offset the $300,000 income inclusion entirely, eliminating the income tax that would otherwise be due.

Direct Beneficiary vs. Estate

You can name a charity as the direct beneficiary of an RRSP or RRIF, bypassing the estate entirely. This is faster (no estate administration delays) and avoids probate fees. However, the tax receipt goes to the estate, not directly to the beneficiary designation. Work with your financial advisor and estate lawyer to ensure the structure achieves your intended result.

TFSA Beneficiary Designations

TFSAs are not subject to the same income inclusion on passing — the assets pass to beneficiaries generally free of tax. Naming a charity as beneficiary of a TFSA generates a donation receipt but doesn't offset a tax liability. Accordingly, RRSPs and RRIFs are generally the more tax-efficient vehicles for charitable beneficiary designations.

Who Should Consider This Strategy?

This strategy is most powerful for Canadians who: have substantial RRSP/RRIF assets they don't expect to fully spend in retirement; have charitable intentions as part of their estate plan; and want to maximize the portion of their estate that goes to causes they care about rather than taxes.

Always work with a qualified estate lawyer and tax professional when establishing beneficiary designations. The interaction between charitable giving, estate administration, and the tax rules is nuanced, and the optimal structure depends on your individual circumstances.

title: Corporate Giving Strategies for Business Owners
excerpt: Business owners have access to giving vehicles that employees don't. From corporate donations to private foundations to the capital gains exemption, here's what advisors need to know.
content:
The Corporate Donor Opportunity

Business owners — whether operating through a corporation, partnership, or self-employment — have access to charitable giving structures that employed individuals don't. Understanding these options is increasingly important as Canada's population of incorporated small business owners continues to grow.

Corporate Donations: The Basics

A Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) can deduct charitable donations at the corporate level, reducing the corporation's taxable income. The deduction limit is 75% of the corporation's net income. Unused charitable donation deductions can be carried forward up to five years.

For many business owners, the question isn't whether to donate personally or corporately — it's both, in the right proportions. Corporate donations are particularly useful when the corporation has retained earnings that would otherwise be subject to the general corporate tax rate.

Gifting Appreciated Private Company Shares

One of the most sophisticated strategies available to business owners involves donating shares of a private company to a charity or DAF. Unlike publicly traded shares, private shares do not qualify for the zero capital gains inclusion rate — but there are other structures, including donated shares to certain foundations, that can achieve tax efficiency in the right circumstances. This is a complex area requiring specialized legal and tax advice.

The Employee Giving Program

Business owners who want to engage their workforce can establish corporate matching programs, payroll deduction programs, or team volunteer events connected to corporate donations. Beyond the tax deduction, these programs tend to improve employee engagement and retention — a consideration worth its own ROI analysis.

Corporate Foundation vs. DAF

Larger businesses sometimes establish a corporate foundation — a private foundation that is funded by the corporation and distributes grants to charities aligned with the company's values. However, the administrative cost and compliance burden of a private foundation is significant. For most businesses, a donor-advised fund held at a community foundation achieves similar results at far lower cost and complexity.

Working With Advisors

Business owners need a coordinated team — accountant, tax lawyer, and financial advisor — to optimize their charitable giving strategy. The interaction between corporate income, shareholder withdrawals, capital gains, and charitable deductions is genuinely complex, and the best outcomes come from planning that considers all of these elements together rather than in isolation.

title: The Difference Between a Foundation and a Registered Charity
excerpt: People often use 'foundation' and 'charity' interchangeably, but they mean different things in Canadian law. Here's what distinguishes them — and why it matters.
content:
Why the Terminology Matters

In casual conversation, 'charity' and 'foundation' are often used interchangeably. In Canadian law, they're distinct categories — and understanding the difference helps you make better decisions as a donor and better understand the organizations you support.

The CRA's Three Categories

The CRA recognizes three types of registered charities: charitable organizations, public foundations, and private foundations. All three can issue official donation receipts. All three must have exclusively charitable purposes. But they differ in structure, funding, and governance.

Charitable Organizations

Charitable organizations are generally hands-on service providers — they directly deliver programs or services. Most of the charities Canadians know by name (cancer societies, food banks, hospitals, schools) are charitable organizations. They typically derive more than 50% of their funding from arm's-length sources and have boards with no more than 50% non-arm's-length members.

Public Foundations

Public foundations primarily make grants to other registered charities rather than running their own programs. They raise money from a broad public base. Community foundations — like the Vancouver Foundation, Calgary Foundation, and Toronto Foundation — are public foundations, as are many donor-advised fund vehicles. The Trillium Foundation and other grant-making organizations typically fall into this category.

Private Foundations

Private foundations are controlled by a family or small group — think the Weston Foundation, the McConnell Foundation, or smaller family philanthropy vehicles. They're primarily funded by a single source (the founding family or corporation), make grants rather than running programs, and are subject to more stringent CRA oversight due to the concentration of control. They cannot accumulate assets without a clear distribution plan.

What This Means for Donors

Most donors can give to all three types and receive tax receipts in all cases. The distinction matters more when you're deciding where to place a large gift — particularly if you're considering establishing a fund within a public foundation versus establishing your own private foundation. Cost, governance, control, and grantmaking flexibility all differ meaningfully between these options.

The DAF Middle Path

For donors who want some of the structure and flexibility of a private foundation without the administrative burden, a donor-advised fund within a public foundation is increasingly the preferred option. You get strategic grantmaking, some control over investment direction, and a charitable receipt — without the need to register and administer a separate legal entity.

title: Charitable Bequests: The Gift That Outlives You
excerpt: A charitable bequest in your will is the most common form of legacy giving in Canada. Here's what you need to know — and the language to use when drafting yours.
content:
What Is a Charitable Bequest?

A charitable bequest is a gift made through your will to a registered charity. It takes effect after your passing and can take the form of a specific amount of money, a percentage of your estate, a specific asset (such as a piece of art or real estate), or the residue of your estate after other bequests are distributed.

Bequests are the most common form of legacy giving in Canada. According to research by CanadaHelps, Canadians who include a charitable bequest in their will leave an average gift of approximately $35,000 — and the cumulative impact on the charitable sector is significant. Every year, thousands of Canadians make a lasting difference through their estates.

Types of Bequests

A specific bequest designates a fixed dollar amount or specific asset: "I give $25,000 to the Canadian Cancer Society." A residual bequest gives a percentage or all of what remains after other estate obligations are met: "I give 20% of the residue of my estate to the Heart & Stroke Foundation." A contingent bequest provides a gift only if another condition is met — for example, if a primary beneficiary does not survive you.

The Tax Advantages

A charitable bequest made through your will generates a donation tax credit on your final return and in the preceding year. The estate can claim credits up to 100% of the deceased's net income in those years. This means a substantial estate gift can effectively eliminate income tax on the final return, including the deemed disposition of RRSPs, RRIFs, and capital property.

Drafting Language

When updating your will to include a charitable bequest, accuracy matters. Include the full legal name of the charity, its CRA Business Number, and a condition specifying the purpose of the gift (if desired). Sample language: "I give and bequeath the sum of [AMOUNT] to [FULL LEGAL NAME OF CHARITY], a registered charity (BN: XXX-XXX-XXX RR 000X), to be used for [its general purposes / the specific program X]."

Let the Charity Know

You're under no obligation to notify a charity of a bequest in advance. But many people choose to do so — and charities deeply appreciate hearing about intended gifts. It allows them to acknowledge your generosity, provide any information that might be helpful (like current programs), and maintain the relationship. It may also encourage you to stay connected to the organization over time.

title: Donor-Advised Funds vs. Private Foundations: Which Is Right for You?
excerpt: For high-net-worth Canadians with serious charitable intentions, the choice between a donor-advised fund and a private foundation is one of the most consequential giving decisions you'll make.
content:
The Core Trade-Off

Both donor-advised funds (DAFs) and private foundations allow wealthy Canadians to structure their philanthropy, make grants to charities they care about, and take tax receipts at the time of contribution. The differences lie in control, cost, privacy, flexibility, and administrative burden — and they're significant.

Donor-Advised Funds: The Case For

A DAF is established within an existing public foundation — a community foundation or national DAF sponsor. You make an irrevocable contribution and receive an immediate tax receipt. The sponsoring organization handles all legal, administrative, and compliance work. You recommend grants over time. Annual administrative fees typically run 0.5–1.0% of assets.

DAFs are private — your grants do not have to be publicly disclosed. They can be established with as little as $10,000–$25,000 in many programs. You can donate cash, publicly traded securities, or other eligible assets. The entire structure is ready to use within days of your initial contribution.

Private Foundations: The Case For

A private foundation is a separate legal entity — a corporation or trust — that you control entirely. You determine investment policy, grantmaking priorities, and governance. You can employ family members in meaningful roles. The foundation's name can reflect your family's legacy. You can engage in proactive grantmaking and relationship-building with charities in ways that DAF sponsors may not facilitate.

Private foundations must distribute at least 3.5% of their assets annually to qualified donees. They are subject to regulatory restrictions on self-dealing, accumulation of assets, and political activities. They must file public T3010 returns, which means your grantmaking is publicly disclosed. Setup costs often exceed $10,000–$20,000, and ongoing compliance, accounting, and administrative costs can reach $15,000–$30,000+ per year.

The Decision Framework

In general: if you have less than $1–2 million to deploy philanthropically, a DAF is almost always the better choice. The administrative cost savings and simplicity far outweigh any reduction in control. If you have $5M+ and strong preferences about family involvement, named legacy, or highly customized grantmaking, a private foundation may be worth the overhead. Between $2–5M is the grey zone where the decision depends heavily on your specific priorities.

Hybrid Approaches

Some major donors use both — maintaining a DAF for straightforward annual grantmaking and a private foundation for family engagement, staffed program work, or specialized philanthropy. This isn't unusual among families with $10M+ in philanthropic assets. Work with an advisor who specializes in philanthropic planning to determine what combination, if any, makes sense for your situation.

title: Securities Donations: A Step-by-Step Guide for Canadians
excerpt: Donating publicly traded securities directly eliminates capital gains tax entirely. Here's the exact process — from initiating the transfer to receiving your receipt.
content:
Why Securities Donations Beat Cash

When you donate appreciated publicly traded securities directly to a registered charity — without selling them first — two powerful tax benefits combine. First, the capital gains inclusion rate on those securities drops to zero (from the standard 50%). Second, you receive a donation receipt for the full fair market value of the shares on the date of transfer.

This combination makes securities donations among the most tax-efficient charitable strategies available to Canadians with non-registered investment accounts holding unrealized gains.

Step 1: Contact the Charity

Call or email the charity's major gifts or planned giving team. Explain that you want to make a gift of securities. They'll provide their brokerage account details: the institution name, account number, and DTC number (for Canadian accounts, this may involve Cédéo or CDS instructions depending on the broker).

Step 2: Contact Your Broker

With the charity's transfer instructions in hand, contact your investment advisor or call your brokerage directly. Ask to initiate an in-kind securities transfer to the charity's account. Emphasize the phrase "in-kind" — you want the shares transferred, not sold. Provide the charity's full brokerage account information.

Most major brokers (TD, RBC, Scotia, BMO, CIBC, Fidelity, Charles Schwab Canada) handle this regularly. Ask your broker for an estimated settlement timeline — typically 3–7 business days for Canadian securities.

Step 3: Confirm the FMV

The donation receipt will be for the fair market value on the date the securities are received into the charity's account — not the date you initiate the transfer. Track the share price on the settlement date. Some charities calculate FMV using the average of the high and low prices on the receipt date; this is acceptable CRA practice.

Step 4: Receive Your Receipt

The charity will issue a receipt for the FMV of the transferred securities. This receipt is claimed on your tax return like any donation receipt. You report zero capital gains on the transferred shares — the T5008 your broker issues showing the proceeds of disposition should reflect a zero or nominal proceeds figure for in-kind transfers.

Year-End Timing

Initiate in-kind transfers by mid-December to ensure settlement before December 31. Transfers that settle in January generate receipts for the following tax year. Given back-office delays at year-end, build in at least two weeks of buffer. When in doubt, call both the charity and your broker to confirm the expected settlement date.

Mutual Funds and ETFs

The zero-inclusion rule also applies to mutual fund units and ETFs held in non-registered accounts. The same in-kind transfer process applies, though some mutual fund companies require additional authorization for direct transfers to charities. Check with your fund company in advance.

title: Estate Planning and Charitable Giving: What Every Canadian Needs to Know
excerpt: Your estate plan is the final and often largest expression of your philanthropic values. Here's how to integrate charitable giving into your estate strategy in a way that's both meaningful and tax-efficient.
content:
Why Estate Planning and Philanthropy Belong Together

For most Canadians, the largest gift they'll ever make to charity happens at or after the time of their passing. Legacy gifts — bequests, RRSP/RRIF beneficiary designations, life insurance proceeds — can dwarf a lifetime of annual donations. And yet most people never plan them intentionally.

The good news: a properly structured estate plan can significantly reduce — and in some cases eliminate — the income tax owing on your final return, while directing more of your lifetime wealth to causes you care about.

Key Tools in the Estate Planning Toolkit

Charitable bequests in your will are the foundation — a direct, legally binding expression of your philanthropic intentions. Beyond that: RRSP and RRIF beneficiary designations to charity can offset the income tax triggered by deemed disposition. Life insurance policies can be structured to donate the death benefit to charity (you receive donation receipts for premiums paid). Real property, art, and other capital assets can be gifted to charities or foundations.

The Deemed Disposition Challenge

When a Canadian passes away, the CRA treats the event as if all assets were sold at fair market value on the date of passing. Capital gains on appreciated securities, real estate (other than a principal residence), and other capital assets are all triggered. Combined with RRSP/RRIF deemed income, the tax on a final return can be substantial.

Strategic charitable gifting in your estate plan can neutralize much of this tax through the 100% net income offset available to estates for charitable donations in the year of passing and the year preceding. This is the core of estate charitable planning: matching the tax-generating events with offsetting charitable donation credits.

Working With Your Estate Team

Effective estate charitable planning requires coordination among an estate lawyer (who drafts the will and beneficiary designations), a tax accountant (who models the tax outcomes under different scenarios), and a financial advisor (who identifies which assets are most tax-efficient to donate).

Don't forget to review your estate plan after major life changes: marriage, separation, a new child or grandchild, significant changes in asset values, or major changes in tax law. Estate plans that haven't been reviewed in 5+ years may not reflect your current wishes or the current tax environment.

The Conversation With Your Family

One of the most important steps in legacy philanthropy is having an open conversation with your family about your intentions. Beneficiaries who understand and share your values are more likely to carry your philanthropic legacy forward. Unexpected charitable bequests — or unexpectedly large ones — can create family conflict. Clarity in advance reduces the risk.

title: What Happens to Your Giving When You Pass Away
excerpt: A practical guide to ensuring your charitable intentions survive your passing — from updating beneficiary designations to writing letters of wishes that guide your estate's philanthropy.
content:
Your Giving Doesn't Have to End

One of the most meaningful things a committed donor can do is ensure that their charitable values continue to shape the world after their passing. This isn't just about leaving a bequest — it's about building a complete picture of your philanthropic intentions that your estate and loved ones can follow.

Beneficiary Designations: The Most Direct Tool

Assets with direct beneficiary designations — life insurance policies, RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, and certain pension plans — pass outside your estate and outside your will. This means they transfer quickly (often within weeks), avoid probate fees, and can be directed to charity without going through estate administration.

To donate these assets to charity, simply name the charity as a direct beneficiary. For RRSPs and RRIFs, the tax benefit is powerful: the deemed income inclusion is offset by a donation credit on your final return. For TFSAs, there's no income tax trigger — but the donation receipt still has value if there are other taxable events on the final return.

Letters of Wishes

A letter of wishes is a non-binding document that accompanies your will. It communicates your philanthropic values to your executor and beneficiaries — why certain charities matter to you, how you hope the gifts will be used, what causes you want the family to consider continuing to support. Unlike your will, it doesn't require legal formalities and can be updated easily.

Many planned giving officers at charities are willing to help you write or refine a letter of wishes if you inform them of your intentions in advance.

Endowment Funds

If you want your charitable giving to continue in perpetuity — not just at the time of your passing, but for decades or generations — consider leaving a bequest that establishes a named endowment fund at a community foundation or charity. Endowment funds invest the principal and distribute only the income (typically 3–5% per year), meaning the capital base remains intact indefinitely.

A $100,000 endowment at 4% annual distribution generates $4,000 per year in perpetuity — potentially supporting causes you care about for centuries.

Updating Your Plan Regularly

Estate plans become outdated. Charities merge, change their mandates, or occasionally lose their charitable status. BN numbers and legal names change. Review your estate's charitable designations every three to five years and after any significant life event. Confirm that the organizations you've named still exist and still align with your values.

title: What Is a Charitable Gift Annuity?
excerpt: A charitable gift annuity provides lifetime income in exchange for a charitable gift. Here's how they work in Canada and when they make sense.
content:
The Basic Concept

A charitable gift annuity is an arrangement in which a donor transfers a sum of money or property to a registered charity, and in return receives fixed periodic payments (typically quarterly or monthly) for the rest of their life. Part of each payment is treated as a return of capital (tax-free), part as interest income (taxable), and part — the difference between the payments received and the actuarial value of those payments — as a charitable donation.

How the Tax Treatment Works

When you establish a gift annuity, the charity calculates the present value of the annuity payments it will make to you (using CRA-prescribed mortality tables and interest rates). The excess of your initial contribution over this present value is the charitable portion — and you receive a donation receipt for that amount.

For example, if you contribute $100,000 and the actuarial value of the lifetime payments is calculated at $70,000, you receive a donation receipt for $30,000 immediately. Each payment you receive is then partly tax-free return of capital and partly taxable interest.

Who Charitable Gift Annuities Are For

This strategy works best for older donors — typically 70+ — who have assets they don't expect to need for capital purposes, want guaranteed income for life, and have charitable intentions. The older the annuitant, the higher the payment rate (because life expectancy is shorter) and the larger the charitable portion of the initial gift.

Gift annuities are also attractive to donors with highly appreciated assets who want income. By donating appreciated securities to fund the annuity, you combine the capital gains benefit of a direct securities donation with the income stream of the annuity.

Canadian Availability

Charitable gift annuities are not as widely offered in Canada as in the United States. A relatively small number of large charities and planned giving programs administer them directly. Donors interested in gift annuities should contact the planned giving office of their preferred charity — or speak with an advisor who specializes in planned giving structures.

Comparison to Other Income Strategies

Compared to a purchased commercial annuity, a charitable gift annuity typically pays a lower income stream (because part of the contribution funds the charitable gift). The trade-off is the immediate tax receipt and the satisfaction of making a meaningful gift. For donors who want both income and philanthropy, it can be an elegant solution — but the math should be reviewed carefully against alternatives.

title: Recurring Giving: Why Monthly Donors Are a Charity's Best Friend
excerpt: A $25/month commitment is worth more to a charity than a $200 one-time gift. Here's the math — and why setting up a monthly donation is one of the best things you can do for a cause you care about.
content:
The Value of Predictability

Charities run programs. Programs require staff. Staff need to be hired and retained. None of this can happen if the organization doesn't know whether it can make payroll six months from now. The single biggest operational challenge for most Canadian charities isn't finding donors — it's the unpredictability of one-time donations that makes planning so difficult.

A committed monthly donor changes this equation entirely. When a charity knows it has 5,000 people giving $25 per month, it can plan. It can hire. It can make multi-year program commitments that actually produce lasting change. This is why monthly giving is, quite genuinely, the most valuable form of donation for most organizations.

The Math Is Compelling

Consider the difference between a $200 one-time donation and a $25/month recurring commitment. Year one: the recurring donor gives $300, already more than the one-time gift. Year three: $900. Year five: $1,500. And the recurring donor is also more likely to increase their gift, respond to emergency appeals, and leave a bequest.

Charities know this — which is why they invest heavily in converting one-time donors to monthly givers. When a charity asks you to consider a monthly gift instead of a single donation, they're not being greedy. They're showing you what would actually help them most.

What Monthly Giving Does for You

Beyond the impact, monthly giving has advantages for donors. Your tax receipt comes at year-end as a single consolidated receipt (most charities will send one receipt for your cumulative annual giving). You don't face the cognitive burden of deciding whether to give each time. You build a sustainable relationship with an organization you care about. And many donors report that automated monthly giving actually increases their overall giving — because the habit expands rather than replacing what they'd give anyway.

How to Set It Up

Most charities make monthly giving extremely simple — typically a checkbox or toggle on their donation page. Your credit card or bank account is charged automatically on the same date each month. You can change the amount, pause, or cancel at any time. You're never locked in.

A Practical Suggestion

If you're currently giving to one or two charities through occasional one-time gifts, consider consolidating those gifts into a single monthly commitment to each organization. If you're giving $200–$300 per year to a charity, a $25/month commitment is approximately equivalent and far more useful to the organization. Make the call today — most charities have a simple process to convert you, and they will genuinely thank you for it.

title: How to Talk to Your Family About Charitable Giving
excerpt: Charitable giving can feel deeply personal — and bringing family members into the conversation requires care, openness, and good timing. Here's how to start.
content:
Why the Conversation Is Worth Having

Philanthropy is most sustainable when it's shared. Couples who give together tend to give more, more intentionally, and over longer periods than those who give separately or without discussion. Parents who involve children in giving decisions are more likely to raise children who give as adults. And families who discuss charitable intentions openly avoid the misunderstandings and conflict that often arise around estate giving.

Starting With Your Partner or Spouse

If you and your partner haven't aligned on your giving philosophy, start with curiosity rather than persuasion. Ask: Are there causes that matter to you personally? Is there an amount that feels right? What organizations do you already trust? Many couples discover they share more charitable values than they realized — they just haven't talked about it.

A practical exercise: each of you independently writes down three causes you care about and an amount you'd be comfortable giving annually. Share the lists and look for overlap. In most cases, there's significant alignment — and the gaps are negotiable.

Introducing Children to Giving

Research consistently shows that charitable giving habits form early. Children who participate in giving decisions — even small ones — are significantly more likely to be generous adults. Start simple: give your child a small amount at the holiday season and let them choose an organization to donate it to. Discuss why they chose what they chose. As they get older, involve them in researching charities, attending charity events, or volunteering alongside family giving.

The goal isn't to impose your charitable values on your children — it's to model generosity and help them develop their own.

Discussing Legacy Giving With Aging Parents

One of the most challenging but important conversations is about legacy giving — particularly if an aging parent has charitable intentions that haven't been formally documented. These conversations are easier when framed around values and stories rather than dollars. Ask: Were there causes that mattered to you over your life? Are there organizations you'd want to support through your estate? What impact do you want to leave?

Many families find these conversations more meaningful than they expected — and they can prevent significant misunderstandings at the time of estate administration.

When Families Disagree

Disagreements about giving are normal. One partner may want to give locally, another internationally. One sibling may want to support causes the others don't. These differences don't have to be resolved through compromise that makes everyone slightly unhappy — many families find it works better to allow each person an individual allocation for personal giving, alongside a shared family giving commitment for causes everyone agrees on.

title: Tax Credits for Charitable Giving: A Province-by-Province Guide
excerpt: Your charitable donation tax credit isn't the same in every province. Here's a complete breakdown of federal and provincial rates — and how they stack to reduce your tax bill.
content:
Federal Credits: The Foundation

Before looking at provincial credits, it's important to understand the federal base. The federal charitable donation tax credit provides:

  • 15% on the first $200 of total donations claimed in a tax year
  • 29% on amounts above $200
  • 33% on amounts above $200 if your income qualifies for the 33% federal bracket (income above $235,675 in 2024)

These are non-refundable tax credits — they reduce the tax you owe, but if your credits exceed your tax owing, you don't receive a refund.

Provincial Credits Add Significantly

Every province has its own charitable donation tax credit that stacks on top of the federal amount. Provincial rates (on the first $200 and amounts above) vary meaningfully by province. Here's the breakdown for amounts above $200 — where most of your giving impact occurs:

  • Ontario: 11.16% provincial credit above $200 (combined federal+provincial = ~40.16%)
  • British Columbia: 16.8% provincial above $200 (combined ~45.8%)
  • Alberta: 21% provincial above $200 (combined ~50%, one of the highest in Canada)
  • Quebec: 24% provincial above $200 (combined ~53%, highest in Canada)
  • Manitoba: 17.4% provincial above $200
  • Saskatchewan: 14.5% provincial above $200
  • Nova Scotia: 21% provincial above $200
  • New Brunswick: 19.5% provincial above $200
  • Prince Edward Island: 16.7% provincial above $200
  • Newfoundland and Labrador: 21.3% provincial above $200

What This Means in Practice

A $1,000 donation by an Ontario donor generates approximately $30 (federal, first $200) + $232 (federal, next $800) + $89 (provincial, next $800) = approximately $351 in total tax credits. Their after-tax cost of giving is $1,000 - $351 = $649.

The same $1,000 donation by a Quebec donor generates a total credit of approximately $421 — an after-tax cost of $579. Quebec donors get the highest combined credit in Canada, which is worth understanding when planning significant gifts.

Claim on the Right Return

Spouses can combine all donation receipts and claim them on either return. It's almost always optimal to claim on the higher-income spouse's return to access the higher federal rate above $200 — and particularly the 33% rate if applicable. Work with your accountant to optimize the allocation each year.

title: Charitable Giving for Newcomers to Canada
excerpt: If you're new to Canada, the charitable giving system here may be different from what you're used to. This guide explains how it works — and how you can make a difference from day one.
content:
Welcome to Canada's Charitable Sector

Canada has one of the most developed charitable sectors in the world. There are approximately 86,000 registered charities serving virtually every cause imaginable — from local food banks to international relief organizations. For newcomers, navigating this landscape and understanding how to give effectively can feel unfamiliar. This guide is here to help.

How Canadian Tax Receipts Work

When you donate to a registered Canadian charity, you receive an official donation receipt that you can use to claim tax credits on your Canadian tax return. This is a significant benefit: a $500 donation can reduce your federal and provincial taxes by $150 or more, depending on your province and income.

To claim these credits, you must file a Canadian tax return. If you arrived partway through the year, you can claim donations made after your arrival date on your first partial-year return. Keep every receipt.

Giving to Organizations in Your Home Country

Canada has a limited number of tax treaties that allow Canadians to claim donations to foreign charities. Outside of the United States (where a treaty exists with specific conditions), donations to most foreign organizations do not generate a Canadian tax receipt. If you want to support causes in your home country and receive a Canadian tax benefit, look for Canadian organizations that fund international programs — many international development charities (World Vision Canada, Oxfam Canada, Islamic Relief Canada) work globally and are registered in Canada.

Finding Community Organizations

Many immigrant communities in Canada have established cultural associations and charitable organizations that support newcomers, preserve cultural heritage, and fund community services. These organizations are often registered charities and serve as important community hubs. Check with your local settlement organization or newcomer centre for a list of community-based charities in your area.

Volunteering as a Form of Giving

If you're not yet in a position to donate financially, volunteering is a deeply valued contribution to the Canadian charitable sector. Charities rely on volunteers for everything from food bank operations to fundraising events. Volunteering is also an excellent way to build your Canadian network, practice French or English in a supportive environment, and find causes you care enough about to support financially later.

No Minimum to Start

There is no minimum donation required to support a Canadian charity. Official receipts are issued for gifts of $10 or more, but many charities will accept any amount. You don't need to be wealthy to make a difference. Start where you are, with what you have.

title: What Is Impact Investing? And How Is It Different From Charity?
excerpt: Impact investing and charitable giving both aim to do good — but they're fundamentally different tools. Here's how to think about each, and whether you should do both.
content:
Two Different Tools for Good

Impact investing and charitable giving are both ways to align your financial decisions with your values. But they operate differently, serve different purposes, and reach different parts of the problem spectrum. Understanding the distinction makes you a more effective philanthropist — and a better investor.

What Is Impact Investing?

Impact investing means deploying capital with the intention of generating measurable positive social or environmental outcomes alongside a financial return. It operates in the investment space — not the grant space — and expects capital to be returned (ideally with interest).

Examples in Canada include: community bonds issued by non-profit housing providers, green bonds from municipalities and clean energy companies, community development finance institutions (CDFIs) that lend to underserved communities, and increasingly, ESG-screened equity and fixed income funds.

What Charitable Giving Does That Impact Investing Cannot

Impact investing works well for problems with business models attached — housing, clean energy, microfinance, fair trade supply chains. But many of the most pressing social problems don't have revenue-generating business models. Food banks, refugee support services, palliative care for the poor, addiction treatment — these require grants, not loans. Only charitable giving can fund these activities at scale.

Impact investing is not a substitute for philanthropy. It's a complement to it. The most sophisticated philanthropists use both tools: grants for work that the market won't fund, and impact investments for opportunities where capital can do good and return.

ESG Investing: Related but Different

ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) investing is a form of impact investing at the public markets level — choosing funds or securities that screen for certain social and environmental criteria. ESG investing has become mainstream, with hundreds of ESG-labelled funds available in Canada.

Critics note that ESG labels are inconsistently applied and that owning ESG funds may not generate meaningfully better outcomes than traditional diversified portfolios. The evidence on ESG investing's real-world impact (as opposed to portfolio performance) is genuinely contested. Treat ESG investing as one tool — not a replacement for direct charitable giving.

The Bottom Line for Donors

If you're already giving charitably and have investment assets, exploring impact investing makes sense as part of a broader values-aligned financial strategy. If you're choosing between giving to charity and impact investing, the needs of the sector strongly favour charitable gifts — particularly for organizations doing work that cannot generate a financial return. Do both if you can.

title: How to Give Anonymously in Canada
excerpt: Many Canadians prefer to give quietly. Here's how to make anonymous donations while still receiving tax receipts — and the options for completely private giving.
content:
Why Some Donors Choose Anonymity

There are many good reasons to give anonymously. Privacy from family members or business associates. Wanting to avoid donor recognition obligations or naming opportunities. Religious or philosophical commitment to giving without recognition. Or simply preferring that charitable giving not attract attention. All of these are valid — and all are achievable under Canadian law.

Anonymous Donations to Charities Directly

Most charities will honour a request for anonymity in their public donor lists and communications. If you donate online, you can typically request anonymous recognition during the donation process. If you give by cheque or bank transfer, you can request in writing that your name not appear in donor lists, annual reports, or public acknowledgements.

The limitation: for you to claim a tax credit, the charity must have your name and address for the receipt. A donation can be publicly anonymous but still tax-receiptable — these are separate things.

Giving Through a Donor-Advised Fund

A donor-advised fund is one of the most effective tools for anonymous giving. You make a contribution to the DAF (and receive a receipt in your name), then recommend grants to charities from the fund. When the DAF's sponsoring organization sends the grant to the charity, it can do so without disclosing your name — the grant appears to come from the foundation, not from you personally.

This is how many large anonymous gifts to hospitals, universities, and community organizations are made. The donor receives their tax receipt privately; the charity sees only the grant from the foundation.

Giving Through Your Employer

If your employer has a workplace giving program or United Way campaign, payroll deductions and workplace gifts are often processed in aggregate — charities receive a bulk payment without individual donor identification. This is a naturally anonymous form of giving.

Cash Gifts

For small gifts where you do not need a tax receipt, cash donations — through a donation box, a church offering, or a direct cash gift — are entirely anonymous by nature. The trade-off is the absence of any tax receipt.

A Final Note

Anonymous giving is honourable and widely practised. Most charities receive a meaningful percentage of their gifts anonymously. If anonymity matters to you, don't let the perceived complexity stop you — a brief conversation with the charity or with your financial advisor will quickly identify the right structure for your situation.

title: Charitable Gifts of Real Estate: What You Need to Know
excerpt: Donating real property to a registered charity is possible and can be highly tax-efficient — but the process is complex and requires careful planning. Here's the complete picture.
content:
Can You Donate Real Estate to a Charity?

Yes — registered Canadian charities can accept gifts of real estate, including residential property, commercial property, vacant land, and shares in a real estate corporation. However, unlike securities donations, gifts of real estate do not qualify for the zero capital gains inclusion rate. The appreciation on donated real property is still subject to capital gains tax at the normal inclusion rate (50%).

Despite this, real estate gifts can still be highly beneficial — particularly for donors who hold investment properties with low original cost bases and want to make a substantial charitable gift without triggering an immediate cash flow obligation.

How the Tax Treatment Works

When you donate real property to a registered charity, the fair market value of the property is used to determine both the capital gain (FMV minus your adjusted cost base) and the donation receipt amount. The capital gain is included in your income at 50%, while the donation receipt generates a credit that can significantly offset that gain and other income.

Example: You donate a property with a cost base of $200,000 and a current FMV of $600,000. You realize a $400,000 capital gain, of which $200,000 is included in income. You also receive a $600,000 donation receipt. At appropriate tax rates, the donation credit will more than offset the capital gains inclusion — meaning you make a $600,000 gift at a very low net tax cost, or even a tax saving.

Getting a Qualified Appraisal

The CRA requires that gifts of real estate be supported by a qualified appraisal from a designated appraiser using standard appraisal methods. The appraisal establishes the FMV used for both the capital gain calculation and the donation receipt. Without a qualified appraisal, the CRA may reassess the gift. Build the cost of an appraisal into your planning.

Practical Considerations

Not all charities can accept real estate — they may lack the resources to manage, sell, or administer property. Confirm in advance that the charity is willing and able to accept your gift. Large charities, hospitals, universities, and community foundations are the most common recipients of real estate gifts. The CRA also imposes a three-year hold period: if a charity disposes of donated property within three years of receipt, the gift may be subject to special rules.

Work With Specialists

Gifts of real estate are among the most complex planned giving transactions available. Always engage a tax lawyer, a qualified appraiser, and the charity's planned giving team simultaneously. This is not a DIY strategy.

title: How Employers Match Charitable Donations in Canada
excerpt: Workplace giving programs are among the most underused benefits in Canada. Here's a complete overview of how corporate matching works — from payroll deduction to submission deadlines.
content:
The Basics of Employer Matching

An employer matching program multiplies the value of your personal donation to a registered charity. You give $50 to a food bank; your employer writes a cheque for another $50 (or $100, depending on the match ratio). The charity receives double — or more — what you gave.

This is one of the purest forms of amplified giving: you're effectively directing your employer's corporate social responsibility budget toward causes you care about, at no additional cost to you.

Common Program Structures

Programs vary significantly by employer. Dollar-for-dollar matching is most common — for every dollar you donate, your employer donates one. Some employers offer 2:1 matching (you give $100, employer gives $200). Some cap the match at a specific annual amount per employee ($1,000, $2,500, or $5,000 are typical ceilings). Some restrict matching to specific categories of charities (registered Canadian charities only, or excluding religious organizations).

Payroll Deduction Programs

Many companies offer payroll deduction giving — you authorize a portion of each paycheque to go directly to one or more registered charities. This is administratively simple, creates a consolidated annual receipt, and often qualifies for corporate matching automatically. The United Way's payroll deduction program is the most widely used in Canada, but many companies extend payroll deduction to a broader range of charities.

How to Submit a Matching Request
