The process typically involves: donating to an eligible charity and obtaining your official tax receipt; logging into your employer's matching portal (common platforms include Benevity, YourCause, and Blackbaud); submitting the receipt information; and waiting for the employer's grant to be processed. Some employers process matches automatically through payroll integration; others require manual submissions. Check your HR portal for specific instructions.

Year-End Deadlines

Many employer matching programs have year-end submission deadlines — often December 31 of the calendar year, or sometimes as early as November 30. Missing the deadline means forfeiting the match. Set a calendar reminder in November to review and submit any outstanding matching requests before the deadline.

If Your Employer Doesn't Have a Program

If your employer doesn't currently offer matching, you can advocate for one. Propose it to HR as part of the company's employee engagement or CSR strategy. Small and mid-sized companies can establish simple matching programs through platforms like Benevity or Canada Helps for Business without significant administrative overhead.

title: The Giving Pledge: What It Is and What It Means for Philanthropy
excerpt: The Giving Pledge — the public commitment by billionaires to donate the majority of their wealth — has reshaped global philanthropic norms. Here's what advisors need to understand about its implications for wealthy Canadian donors.
content:
What Is the Giving Pledge?

The Giving Pledge is a campaign launched in 2010 by Bill Gates, Melinda French Gates, and Warren Buffett. Signatories publicly commit to giving the majority of their wealth to philanthropic causes during their lifetime or at the time of their passing. As of 2025, more than 240 individuals and families from 30+ countries have signed, representing a combined commitment of hundreds of billions of dollars.

Canadian signatories include several prominent business leaders. While the Pledge is U.S.-based and non-binding, it has become a powerful social norm among ultra-high-net-worth individuals worldwide.

Why It Matters for Advisors to Understand

Advisors serving high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients increasingly encounter philanthropic conversations as a core part of wealth planning. The Giving Pledge represents the leading edge of a broader cultural shift: wealthy individuals are increasingly expected — and increasingly choosing — to deploy a significant portion of their assets philanthropically rather than passing everything to heirs.

This shift has implications for estate planning, tax strategy, family governance, and the structure of wealth transfer conversations. Advisors who can engage thoughtfully with these topics are better positioned to serve clients who are thinking in this direction.

The Pledge's Broader Impact

Beyond the direct dollars pledged, the Giving Pledge has had normative effects. Peer pressure among the ultra-wealthy has meaningfully shifted expectations about philanthropic giving at the top of the wealth distribution. It has catalyzed the growth of planned giving infrastructure worldwide, increased public discussion of effective philanthropy, and generated significant media coverage that has made philanthropy more mainstream.

Canadian Context

Canada doesn't have a formal equivalent of the Giving Pledge, though organizations like Philanthropic Foundations Canada and the Community Foundations of Canada have worked to cultivate similar norms among major Canadian donors. The challenge in Canada is partly scale (our wealthiest individuals command far less wealth than their U.S. counterparts) and partly cultural — public declarations about wealth and giving are less common in Canadian culture.

Implications for Client Conversations

For advisors: clients who are aware of the Giving Pledge are often ready to have deeper conversations about their own giving. The Pledge provides a useful frame — "what percentage of your estate do you want to go to charity versus to heirs?" — that can unlock planning that clients have been thinking about but haven't put into words. Use it as an entry point, not a prescription.

title: Building a Family Philanthropy Practice
excerpt: The most enduring charitable legacies are built by families who develop a shared practice — not just a plan. Here's how advisors can help clients build something that lasts generations.
content:
Beyond the Bequest

Most estate planning conversations about philanthropy end with a bequest: X percent to charity Y, with the remainder to heirs. This is a good start. But the families whose charitable impact endures across generations aren't just the ones with the biggest bequests — they're the ones who built a practice of giving that the next generation adopted, adapted, and carried forward.

Building that kind of legacy requires intention, conversation, and structure. It's as much about family dynamics and values transmission as it is about tax planning.

The Four Elements of a Family Philanthropy Practice

Advisors who work with multi-generational clients in this space often describe four key elements: shared values (a clearly articulated set of philanthropic priorities that family members have discussed and endorsed), governance (a process for making giving decisions together), education (exposure to philanthropy that builds knowledge and commitment in the next generation), and infrastructure (the legal and financial structures that make sustained giving practical).

Values: The Starting Point

The first conversation in building a family philanthropy practice is always about values, not dollars. What matters to this family? What experiences have shaped their perspective on the world? What change do they most want to see in their lifetime? In their children's lifetime?

These conversations are often facilitated by planned giving advisors, family office staff, or wealth psychologists. They surface consensus — and healthy disagreement — that must be worked through before any structure is established. Rushing to the structure before the values are clear is the most common reason family philanthropy programs fail.

Governance: Decision-Making That Scales

As families grow, informal decision-making about giving becomes unwieldy. A family giving committee — with clear rules about who can join, how decisions are made, and how the family's philanthropic priorities are reviewed and updated — provides the structure that sustains giving across generations.

Community foundations can provide administrative support for family giving committees within their donor-advised fund programs, which reduces the burden on family members and provides independent governance oversight.

The Role of the Advisor

Advisors who want to add value in this space need to be comfortable facilitating values conversations, not just delivering tax analysis. The families who benefit most from philanthropic planning are those whose advisors treat giving as a first-class financial topic — not an afterthought to estate administration. Bringing in a philanthropy specialist, a community foundation program officer, or a family dynamics facilitator when appropriate can significantly enrich the conversation and the outcomes.
